title: Respond to a new transfusion reaction
stem: During red-cell transfusion, a client develops new chills, fever and back discomfort. Which actions belong in the immediate reaction response? Select all that apply.
options: Discard the bag and tubing immediately.
Give the prescribed antipyretic, then restart the unit once fever settles.
Stop the transfusion and promptly assess the client.
Notify the team and follow the reaction investigation protocol.
Slow the transfusion until the chills settle.
why: The component and set may be needed for investigation; follow the reaction protocol's handling instructions.
A lower temperature does not rule out a serious transfusion reaction or authorize restarting the implicated component; the reaction pathway must guide further decisions.
Further exposure should cease while the new systemic symptoms are assessed for a potentially serious reaction.
Coordinated assessment, samples and product handling help establish the cause and guide treatment.
Reducing the rate still continues exposure to a component that may be causing a serious reaction.
takeaway: Further exposure should cease while the new systemic symptoms are assessed for a potentially serious reaction.
learningObjective: Initiate the transfusion-reaction pathway when new systemic symptoms develop during blood administration.

title: Recognize systemic local-anesthetic toxicity
stem: During a local-anesthetic procedure, a client develops ringing ears, metallic taste and slurred speech. Which priority actions address possible systemic local-anesthetic toxicity? Select all that apply.
options: Ask the client to practise slow breathing for procedural anxiety.
Offer a brief pause and then complete the remaining anesthetic dose.
Alert the procedural team and stop further anesthetic administration.
Prepare airway and circulatory support according to the emergency protocol.
Check capillary glucose as the initial response to the speech change.
why: Anxiety support may help distress but is not an adequate response to these drug-related neurological warning symptoms.
Resuming exposure before the team resolves the suspected toxicity could worsen the event.
Tinnitus, metallic taste and slurred speech can be early systemic toxicity; preventing further exposure is urgent.
Toxicity can progress to seizures and cardiac instability, so early resuscitation readiness matters.
Glucose may help evaluate altered neurological status, but the characteristic symptoms during anesthetic administration require stopping exposure and preparing emergency support first.
takeaway: Tinnitus, metallic taste and slurred speech can be early systemic toxicity; preventing further exposure is urgent.
learningObjective: Respond to early neurological warning symptoms during local-anesthetic administration.

title: Latent tuberculosis before biologic therapy
stem: A client with rheumatoid arthritis feels well and is scheduled to start a tumour necrosis factor inhibitor. They ask why tuberculosis screening was ordered when they have no cough. Which explanation is best?
options: It creates a comparison result for any future TB exposure.
It predicts whether TB will be acquired during future treatment.
It measures how much protection remains from childhood BCG vaccination.
It identifies latent infection that the medicine could reactivate.
why: A baseline can be useful, but the immediate purpose is to address infection already present before immunosuppression.
Screening evaluates evidence of infection already present; it does not predict every future exposure or acquisition.
Latent-TB screening is not a measurement of remaining BCG protection; vaccination history and interpretation of specific test results are separate considerations.
TB may be present without cough or other symptoms; identifying it permits a prevention or treatment plan before TNF inhibition.
takeaway: TB may be present without cough or other symptoms; identifying it permits a prevention or treatment plan before TNF inhibition.
learningObjective: Explain why tuberculosis screening matters before tumour necrosis factor inhibitor therapy.
